paras: The lynching of George Kennedy took place on the night of Sunday, October 18, 1903, when a mob hanged Kennedy, a Black man, to a tree near Taylortown in Bossier Parish, Louisiana. White papers said he had been captured at the Taylortown railroad depot with a pistol, waiting to kill Mercer Brittain, a conductor on the Red River Valley railroad. The story ran as a short wire item in papers as far away as New York and Minnesota, and an Oklahoma paper called the lynching of a man for a contemplated crime "a dangerous precedent."

According to the Colfax Chronicle, Kennedy, whom it called "a negro gambler and tough," had tried to kill Brittain "a day or two before" after the conductor put him out of the white passenger coach. The Alexandria Gazette placed that earlier incident on the evening before the lynching, saying Kennedy tried to shoot the conductor on the train and was stopped by passengers. A Shreveport dispatch was more guarded, saying only that "it is said" Kennedy had made "a murderous assault" on Brittain, and none of the reports named a witness to the encounter.

On the Sunday night, according to the reports, Kennedy was found at the Taylortown depot armed with a pistol, waiting for Brittain to pass on the night train. A New Orleans wire said that "a party of citizens who were informed of the threat" went to the depot and captured him, while the Chronicle spoke of his "being arrested" without saying by whom. The reports had Kennedy openly declaring his purpose; the Gazette said he "expressed joy" at the plan and confessed he meant to kill Brittain "for revenge." The Chronicle wrote that the crowd grew "so enraged at his insolence and bravado" that it decided to hang him "as an example to such desperadoes."

The mob took Kennedy from the depot and hanged him to a tree, about a mile away according to the wire and two miles from Taylortown according to the Gazette. The Chronicle put the hanging at about nine o'clock that night, and the Gazette added that he was given time to say his prayers. The Shreveport dispatch gave the mob as 100 men and reported that it "dispersed quietly."

No report of an inquest, arrest or grand jury inquiry appears in the coverage, and no paper named any member of the mob. Early in November a report of another hanging at Taylortown, that of Joe Craddock, described it as "the second lynching within a month" there.

All of the coverage found came from white papers, which carried the lynching mainly through two short dispatches: a New Orleans wire printed by The Sun of New York and the Minneapolis Journal on October 21, and a Shreveport dispatch in the Bryan Morning Eagle the same day. The wire's charge, "lying in wait with intent to commit murder," was repeated in a news digest in the Kanabec County Times on October 23. Headlines took the accusation as given: The Sun's read "Lynched a Murderously Inclined Negro," and the Minneapolis Journal's subhead "Negro Said He Would Kill White and Is Strung Up."

The earliest item found, a paragraph among the Alexandria Gazette's "Telegraphic Brevities" on October 20, called Kennedy "a negro desperado" and gave the mob as one thousand men. The Colfax Chronicle, which wrote simply of "Bossier citizens," ran the fullest account on October 24 under the headline "A Murderous Negro Lynched" and alone tied the quarrel to Kennedy's removal from the white coach. The only comment found came from the Daily Ardmoreite, which allowed that lynching a man for "contemplating the assassination of a white man" saved the white man "a great deal of trouble" but said it set "a dangerous precedent."

Accounts differed on the size of the mob: 100 men in the Shreveport dispatch, one thousand in the Alexandria Gazette, and an unnumbered "party of citizens" or "crowd" in the wire and the Chronicle. The date also varied, since the wire said "yesterday" under datelines of October 20 and 21, while three separate reports, including the Shreveport dispatch, placed the hanging on Sunday night.

accounts.label: New Orleans wire
accounts.gist: Kennedy was found at the Taylortown depot armed and openly intending to kill Brittain; citizens informed of the threat captured him and hanged him about a mile away.

accounts.label: Shreveport dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of 100 lynched him Sunday night; 'it is said' he had earlier assaulted the conductor and was then found lying in wait; the mob dispersed quietly.

accounts.label: Alexandria Gazette brief
accounts.gist: A mob of one thousand hanged him two miles from Taylortown after he was caught waiting to kill Brittain 'for revenge'; he was given time to pray; the evening before, passengers stopped him from shooting the conductor on the train.

accounts.label: Colfax Chronicle
accounts.gist: A crowd of Bossier citizens hanged him about nine o'clock Sunday night, enraged at his 'insolence and bravado' after his arrest; he had tried to kill Brittain a day or two before for putting him out of the white coach.

framing.detail: The Sun and Minneapolis Journal ran the New Orleans wire under 'Lynched a Murderously Inclined Negro' and 'Lynched for a Threat'; the Kanabec County Times condensed it in a digest.
The Bryan Morning Eagle's Shreveport dispatch, headed 'George Kennedy, Colored, Victim of Wrath of a Mob,' attributed the earlier assault to hearsay ('It is said').
The Colfax Chronicle headed it 'A Murderous Negro Lynched,' called Kennedy 'a negro gambler and tough' and repeated that he was hanged 'as an example to such desperadoes.'
The Alexandria Gazette called him 'a negro desperado' who 'expressed joy' at his planned attack.
The Daily Ardmoreite allowed that the lynching saved the white man 'a great deal of trouble' but said it 'establishes a dangerous precedent.'

conflicts.note: The Shreveport dispatch is the nearest source; the Gazette's figure appears only in a brief digest item.
Three separate reports, including the Shreveport dispatch, give Sunday night; the wire's 'yesterday' shifts with its dateline and looks carried over.
